Great discussion earlier this week on a topic that is only becoming more important.

As AI becomes embedded into the way ideas, content and innovation are created, questions around ownership are only part of the challenge. Being able to evidence how something was developed, who contributed, what tools were used and when key decisions were made is becoming just as important.

That is exactly the infrastructure we are building at Etched Tech.

Thank you Alexander Taylor for hosting, and to everyone who contributed to the discussion. Great to see such a strong conversation developing around evidence, provenance and IP in the AI era.

The Inference Tax: What Trading Systems Reveal About Energy-Aware AI

The fastest accelerator in a two-minute benchmark can become a completely different system forty-five minutes into a live session.
Average latency might hold steady, and mean power may even drop. But the true warning signals show up where it hurts: p99.99 latency, useful output rate, thermal margin, and clock-limit exposure.
That performance gap is the inference tax.

The AI hardware race just got a lot more interesting.

Etched is building the world's first transformer-specific ASIC, the Sohu chip, and their progress update reads like a masterclass in contrarian bets.

The core thesis: GPUs are flexible by design, but that flexibility comes at a cost. Transformers now dominate modern AI, yet we're running them on general-purpose silicon. Etched's answer is to hard-wire the transformer algorithm directly into the chip.

The claim is striking. A single Sohu chip can outperform an entire rack of NVIDIA H100s for inference. Orders of magnitude in performance and energy efficiency, not incremental gains.
